questions.stem: What kind of organism is yeast?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Yeast belongs to the fungi.
Yeast cells live singly.
Fungi form their own kingdom.

questions.stem: Which two respiration modes can yeast carry out?

options.explanation: Photosynthesis never occurs in fungi.
Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Yeast cannot photosynthesise.
The anaerobic mode is essential to bread.

questions.stem: How does yeast access the energy stored in flour?

options.text: It dissolves the flour with acid
options.explanation: Enzymes, not acid, do the digesting.

options.text: It burns the flour directly for heat
options.explanation: Respiration is chemical, not burning.

options.text: Its enzymes break the starch in flour down into usable sugars
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Starch must be digested to sugars first.

questions.stem: When does yeast switch from aerobic to anaerobic respiration in dough?

options.explanation: Aerobic respiration runs first.
Switching happens long before the oven.
Sugar shortage stops all respiration, not just the aerobic mode.

options.text: When the oxygen trapped in the dough runs out
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: A baker's dough smells faintly alcoholic before baking. What explains that?

options.text: Anaerobic respiration in the yeast produced ethanol as well as carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The flour was brewed before milling
options.explanation: Flour processing adds no alcohol.

options.text: The yeast photosynthesised sugars into alcohol
options.explanation: Yeast never photosynthesises.

options.text: Water in the dough fermented by itself
options.explanation: Fermentation needs the yeast cells.

questions.stem: State what yeast is, in biological terms.
questions.modelAnswer: Yeast is a one-cell fungus able to respire both aerobically and anaerobically.

questions.stem: Name the molecule in flour that yeast enzymes break down.
questions.modelAnswer: Enzymes from the yeast break down starch in the flour into sugars for respiration.

questions.stem: Explain why yeast needs both respiration modes during bread making.
questions.modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration supports early growth while oxygen lasts, and anaerobic respiration then keeps the cells alive while producing the carbon dioxide that raises the dough.

questions.stem: A bakery warms its dough room well but seals every bowl tightly. Predict the respiration pattern.
questions.modelAnswer: The yeast will exhaust the trapped oxygen quickly and rely almost entirely on anaerobic respiration, so plenty of carbon dioxide forms but ethanol also accumulates in the sealed bowls.

questions.stem: What makes bread dough rise during proving?

options.text: Water steaming inside the raw dough
options.explanation: Steam matters in the oven, not during proving.

options.text: Carbon dioxide trapped in small air pockets expands the volume
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Yeast cells dividing to fill space
options.explanation: Rising comes from gas, not cell crowding.
Ethanol is liquid, not the lifting gas.

questions.stem: Why does finished bread contain no alcohol?

options.explanation: No absorption claim applies.
No such additive exists in the process.

options.text: The oven heat evaporates the ethanol produced during fermentation
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Anaerobic respiration does produce it.

questions.stem: What happens to the yeast cells during baking?

options.text: They become dormant and revive later
options.explanation: Bread yeast does not revive.

options.text: They multiply faster in the heat
options.explanation: Heat kills rather than multiplies them.
Cells cannot transform into starch.

options.text: The high oven temperature kills them, stopping respiration
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Which respiration product gives the crumb its open texture?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, held in the air pockets set during baking
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Ethanol leaves as vapour without shaping crumb.
Yeast consumes oxygen; it does not release it.
Water contributes crust, not the taught texture.

questions.stem: A baker forgets the yeast entirely. Predict the loaf.

options.text: Rising in the oven by steam
options.explanation: Oven steam cannot replace proving.

options.text: Dense and flat, because no carbon dioxide forms to raise the dough
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Without yeast no gas is generated.
No fermentation means no ethanol either.

questions.stem: State the gas that leavens bread dough and its source.
questions.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide produced by the yeast during anaerobic respiration leavens the dough.

questions.stem: Name the two effects of oven heat on the fermenting dough.
questions.modelAnswer: Baking evaporates the ethanol and kills the yeast cells, ending respiration.

questions.stem: Explain why killing the yeast in the oven is necessary for the finished loaf.
questions.modelAnswer: Dead yeast stops respiration, so the risen shape stays fixed instead of continuing to change, and no further alcohol accumulates in the crumb.

questions.stem: A bakery wants a taller loaf. Apply the gas law of proving to suggest one change.
questions.modelAnswer: Give the dough a longer or warmer prove so the yeast generates more carbon dioxide, filling more air pockets before baking.
